strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: end-to-end agentic LLM fine-tuning (data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement), which is well-motivated as substantially harder than prior MLE benchmarks (MLE-Bench, DSBench, MLE-Dojo) that assume fixed datasets.

FT-Dojo is a reasonably comprehensive environment: 13 tasks across 5 domains, sandboxed Docker execution, modular interfaces (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator), and a pluggable design that supports extension; the two-phase validation/test protocol with strict blind-testing of the test set is well described (Appendix F).

The baseline comparison is thoughtfully controlled: the tool-augmented OpenHands baseline is given identical fine-tuning primitives (LlamaFactoryTool, OpenCompassTool), the same backbone API, the same data repository, the same GPU and 12-hour budget, which strengthens the claim that the gap is architectural rather than tooling-related.

FT-Agent's three mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast progressive validation, structured feedback analysis) are concretely specified, with full prompt architecture in Appendix G, and are each tied to an observed failure mode of generalist agents.

The analysis goes beyond aggregate scores: validation vs. test consistency (Table 5), exploration dynamics (Table 3), effective iteration counts (Table 6), ablations over data scale, agent backbone, and model scale (Table 8), and unusually candid case studies (Table 7, Figures 4-6) that document both success modes (cross-domain data mixing, cumulative learning) and failure modes (shotgun debugging, data collapse from myopic filtering).
The honest treatment of limitations (pattern-matching vs. causal reasoning, planning myopia) and the impact statement discussing dual-use risks of automated fine-tuning are commendable.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is weak relative to the headline claims: test sets are very small (AIME: 15 problems, Visualization: 25, Fact Checking: 48, most others 100), runs appear to be single-seed with no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated trials. The flagship AIME result (13.30% = 2/15 problems) could plausibly be noise, and several table entries differ by single-digit counts.

Potential confound in the main comparison: FT-Agent employs GPT-5 and GPT-4o-mini for data cleaning and synthesis, while the OpenHands baseline is described as using only the GPT-5.2 reasoning endpoint. If OpenHands lacked access to these auxiliary data-processing models, part of the reported gap may reflect resources rather than the agent architecture; this is not clearly controlled.

The Manual SFT baseline behaves implausibly in places (e.g., near-total collapse in Chemistry: 0-10% accuracy, worse than the untuned base model on several tasks), which weakens the 'outperforms human experts' narrative; the 'Two-Pass' constraint also makes it a limited stand-in for expert practice.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the paper relies on proprietary frontier models (agent backbone, data-cleaning models, LLM judge), does not state that FT-Dojo, FT-Agent code, or the sandbox will be publicly released, and does not report decoding parameters, seeds, or judge-model variance, all material for an agent benchmark intended as community infrastructure.

Contamination risk is addressed only briefly: evaluation sets are drawn from established benchmarks (AIME 2025, PANORAMA, TableBench) while training corpora include closely related sources (e.g., DeepScaleR includes AIME 1984-2023); the 'decontamination process' is asserted but its method (n-gram matching? embedding overlap?) is never described.

Ablations cover only 5 of 13 tasks, and some conclusions are under-supported: e.g., 'model-agnostic' generalization is claimed from one 3B model on five tasks; the data-scaling 'quality over quantity' finding rests on mixed results across five tasks with no variance estimates.
The GPT-5-as-judge evaluation for LLM-judged metrics introduces another source of unquantified noise; judge reliability (agreement with human labels) is not reported.

Some quantitative inconsistencies and ambiguities between main text and appendix (e.g., PI4PC where OpenHands leads on validation in Table 5 but ties on test in Table 2; the Reaction task where FT-Agent loses substantially on FTS/BLEU yet the main text emphasizes '10 of 13' wins) suggest the summary metric obscures task-level trade-offs that deserve more prominent discussion.

strengths: The problem framing is genuinely valuable: end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (data construction + training configuration as joint, iterative optimization targets) is a plausible next step beyond MLE-Bench/MLE-Dojo-style fixed-data benchmarks, and FT-Dojo's shared heterogeneous data repository is a meaningful design distinction.

The task suite is diverse (13 tasks, 5 domains) with clear documentation of sources, decontamination, and metric definitions (Appendix A), and the modular sandboxed architecture (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator) is well specified and extensible.

The baseline design shows unusual care: OpenHands is given identical fine-tuning primitives (LlamaFactoryTool, OpenCompassTool), the same data repository, sandbox, backbone, GPU, and 12-hour budget (Appendix B), which strengthens the claim that the gap is architectural rather than tooling.

The case analyses (Figure 4, Table 7, D.1–D.3) are candid and insightful: the 'shotgun debugging' / hedging-language analysis of PI4PC and the data-collapse trace in D.2 are honest negative results that go beyond leaderboard reporting, and the limitations discussion (causal reasoning gaps, planning myopia) is substantive.
Ablations across data scale, agent backbone, and target model size (3B) address generality questions that reviewers of agent-benchmark papers usually have to ask.
weaknesses: Evaluation sets are far too small to support the headline claims. Several tasks have 15–100 test instances (AIME has only 15), so a single problem changes accuracy by 6.7pp. There are no error bars, no multiple runs/seeds, and no significance tests anywhere, yet the paper draws fine-grained conclusions (e.g., FT-Agent 'proves' it can synthesize reasoning trajectories from a 13.30% vs 0.00% difference on a 15-item test—two problems).

The core claim of novelty is overstated. 'No prior work has tackled end-to-end LLM fine-tuning with agents' and 'first interactive benchmark' sit awkwardly against the paper's own citations: LaMDAgent (Yano et al., 2025) optimizes post-training pipelines with agents, and MLE-Dojo is interactive. The genuine delta (open-ended data curation) is real but the framing repeatedly overclaims.

The three proposed mechanisms of FT-Agent (structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, structured feedback analysis) are never ablated individually. Table 3 compares whole systems only, so the paper cannot attribute FT-Agent's gains to its specific design contributions versus, e.g., more loops or better prompts. This is a central missing experiment.

Potential confound in the AIME result: FT-Agent uses GPT-5/4o-mini for data synthesis, and the training repository contains AIME-1984–2023; the claimed decontamination covers raw data, but agent-generated synthetic data is uncontrolled, and the 'all baselines 0%' vs '13.3%' contrast is exactly the kind of result most in need of contamination analysis and repeated runs. None is provided.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Appendix A.4 says AIME/FinanceIQ use 'the standard allocation of 100 samples per split' while Table 1 reports 15 for AIME; Table 2 bolds FT-Agent's PI4PC 44.00 although OpenHands also scores 44.00 (making the '10 of 13' tally ambiguous); the backbone-ablation text cites 'Visualization -16%, Patent -15%' while Table 8 shows Visualization validation actually improving (20→24) under GPT-4o; and 'consistently unlocking significant gains on the smaller 3B model' is contradicted by Finance QA 3B (61.44→60.73 val).

Validation sets of 15–50 instances are also used for model/checkpoint selection, making the selection process itself extremely high variance; the strict blind-test protocol (Appendix F) is commendable but does not fix the noise in the feedback signal agents optimize against.

Cost and compute accounting is incomplete: FT-Agent's iterative-loop cost is reported ($5.73) but the GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini data-synthesis cost is not; the Manual SFT baseline is restricted to two passes with unspecified time/compute, making the human-expert comparison hard to interpret.

Reproducibility is uncertain: the paper does not state whether FT-Dojo, FT-Agent code, prompts beyond the excerpts in Appendix G, or agent logs will be released, and with stochastic agents, frontier-LLM backbones ('GPT-5.2'), and single runs, independent verification would be difficult even with code.

Some claims exceed the evidence stylistically as well as statistically: 'establishes a new state-of-the-art' on the authors' own benchmark, 'exceptional capabilities', and 'proving its ability' are not supported at the reported sample sizes.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: end-to-end autonomous LLM fine-tuning (data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement), which is meaningfully harder and more open-ended than existing MLE benchmarks like MLE-Bench/DSBench that assume fixed datasets. Framing both data strategy and training configuration as first-class optimization targets is a useful and novel contribution.

FT-Dojo is well-designed as a benchmark: modular architecture with clearly defined interfaces (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator), sandboxed reproducible execution, pluggable/extensible task and metric modules, and a two-phase validation/final-assessment protocol with a strict blind-test separation (Appendix F), which guards against test-set overfitting by the agent.

The task suite is diverse (13 tasks, 5 domains, varied metrics from accuracy to Tanimoto similarity and Pass@1) and the appendix provides unusually thorough detail: data sources, decontamination protocol, dataset statistics, baseline implementation, full validation/test tables, complete prompt architecture, and verbatim decision traces (Tables 5-9, Appendix D).

The OpenHands comparison is carefully controlled: identical LLM backbone, identical fine-tuning primitives (LlamaFactory wrappers), identical GPU/time budget, and even injected high-level tools to prevent the baseline from failing on trivial CLI errors. This strengthens the claim that the gap stems from agent architecture rather than tool availability.

The qualitative analyses are a highlight: the contrasting case studies (cumulative learning on Mol_Edit vs. 'shotgun debugging' on PI4PC, data collapse from myopic filtering) are honest, well-evidenced, and provide genuine insight into both capabilities and limitations of current agents rather than only promoting the proposed system.
Ablations cover data scaling, agent backbone, and target model scale, supporting generalization claims beyond a single configuration.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is weak. Several evaluation sets are very small (e.g., AIME valid/test = 15/15; Visualization = 25/25; Fact Checking = 48/48). The headline AIME result (13.30%) corresponds to only 2 of 15 test instances, and the validation counterpart is 20% (3 of 15) — a difference of one or two correct answers. No seeds, variance estimates, or significance tests are reported for any comparison, despite runs being expensive; with 13 tasks this is the paper's most significant evidential gap.

Only one general-purpose agent baseline (OpenHands) is evaluated, plus a constrained Manual SFT. Claims that generalist agents 'fundamentally' fail would be much stronger with additional agent frameworks (e.g., SWE-agent-style scaffolds, AIDE, or the LaMDAgent system cited in related work). The related-work claim that no prior work tackles agent-driven end-to-end fine-tuning sits uneasily alongside the LaMDAgent and MLE-Dojo citations without a sharp empirical comparison.

There is a potential confound in the FT-Agent vs. OpenHands comparison: FT-Agent benefits from domain-specific scaffolding (progressive validation stages, structured feedback schemas, memory of prior experiments) that was co-designed with the benchmark by the same authors. While the paper argues this reflects necessary expert practice, the boundary between 'benchmark contribution' and 'hand-engineered solution to the benchmark' is not sharply drawn, and the generality of the three mechanisms to other environments is untested.

Reproducibility is limited by heavy dependence on proprietary models: GPT-5.2 as the agent backbone, GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini for data synthesis, and GPT-5 as judge for some evaluations. Results may not be reproducible or stable across API versions, and there is no explicit commitment to releasing the FT-Dojo code, data repository, or agent traces.

Some claims are over-strong relative to evidence: 'FT-Agent ensures 100% configuration validity', 'establishes a new state-of-the-art' (on its own new benchmark), and the causal-reasoning conclusions in Section 5/4.4 are drawn from a small number of qualitative traces on two tasks. The hedging-language analysis (Table 7) is interesting but interpretive rather than systematic.

The paper conflates two contributions (benchmark and agent framework), and the headline 'best on 10 of 13' outcome is partly a function of the authors' own agent design choices; a neutral evaluation of multiple agent architectures on FT-Dojo would better establish the benchmark's discriminative value.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark: FT-Dojo formalizes end-to-end LLM fine-tuning as an interactive agent task, going beyond static-dataset benchmarks like MLE-Bench by making data construction, training configuration, and iterative feedback analysis first-class optimization targets. The framing in Section 2.4 ('Benchmark Framing') is honest about what is and is not new.

Careful experimental design: the controlled protocol (identical tools, sandbox, base model, wall-clock budget, and LLM backends for FT-Agent vs. OpenHands) is a genuinely rigorous attempt to isolate the effect of agent design; the appendix documents the harness and prompts in detail, supporting reproducibility.

Useful additional controls: frontier-agent comparisons (Codex, Claude Code), open-source planning backbones, 24-hour budget sensitivity check, LLM-assisted Manual SFT reference, and 3-run statistics for FT-Agent address the most obvious confounds reviewers would raise.

Honest analysis of limitations: the case studies (Section 4.5, Appendix D) candidly expose failure modes such as 'shotgun debugging,' planning myopia, and pattern-matching rather than causal reasoning; the Manual SFT baseline is explicitly scoped as constrained rather than an expert upper bound.

The AIME sparse-supervision finding (agents synthesizing missing CoT supervision where all baselines score 0%) and cross-domain data-mixing behaviors (Appendix D.1) are interesting, well-documented emergent capabilities of practical value.
weaknesses: Statistical power of headline claims is weak: several test sets are tiny (AIME has 15 test instances; Visualization 25; Fact Checking 48). FT-Agent's AIME score of 11.11% ± 3.82 corresponds to roughly 1-2 correct answers out of 15, so 'best on 10 of 13 tasks' can flip with a single instance. No significance testing is provided for the 10/13 claim.

Asymmetric variance reporting: only FT-Agent is run 3 times; all baselines are single runs, yet several FT-Agent advantages are within one standard deviation of the baseline (e.g., Vis 29.33±6.11 vs. 24.00; Reaction metrics with ±11.22 std), undermining the strength of the 10/13 comparison.

Inconsistent numbers across tables: Table 2 reports AIME Test 11.11±3.82 while Table 7 reports 13.30, and Table 4/Table 10 report 13.33 or 20.00 for related settings, with no clear reconciliation of which run/setting each represents. This weakens confidence in reported results.

Potential confound between agent framework and data-synthesis backbone: FT-Agent uses GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini for data cleaning and synthesis while OpenHands uses only GPT-5.2 for reasoning. The LLM-assisted Manual SFT check (Appendix B.1.3) partially addresses this but only on 5 tasks and single runs, so the contribution of the framework per se versus stronger synthesis access is not fully isolated.

Baselines may be under-tuned relative to the scaffolded OpenHands description: while the harness is well-documented, the headline 'OpenHands performs poorly even with strong backends' rests on one harness configuration; robustness of this conclusion across harness variants is untested.
Some reported gains are modest relative to cost and complexity (e.g., Finance QA 67.20 vs. base 65.10), and the paper does not always discuss which wins are practically meaningful.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely relevant and under-explored problem: evaluating language agents on end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement), which existing MLE benchmarks (MLE-Bench, MLE-Dojo) do not directly cover.

The system design is thoughtful: a sandboxed Docker environment with Meta API / Data Repository / Evaluator interfaces, a two-phase validation/test protocol, pluggable task modules, and a shared raw-data repository that makes data selection a first-class optimization target.

The experimental protocol makes a serious attempt at controlled comparison: identical tool wrappers (LlamaFactory/OpenCompass), identical wall-clock budget, extended-budget check (24h OpenHands run), and 3-run statistics for FT-Agent.

The case studies (Appendix C–D) are unusually candid, documenting both cumulative-learning successes (Mol_Edit) and failure modes such as 'shotgun debugging' on PI4PC and myopic filtering data collapse on Visualization; the limitations discussion is honest and substantive.

The ablations (data scaling, planning backbone, target model scale) and the five-task frontier-agent comparison (Codex, Claude Code, open-source backbones) add useful context beyond the headline claim.
weaknesses: Statistical support for the central claims is very weak on several tasks. AIME 2025 has only 15 test instances, so the headline 'breakthrough' of 11.11%±3.82 (best 10-of-13 claim) rests on roughly 1–2 problems, and the val→test drop (20.00→13.30) suggests noise, not signal. Other tasks (Vis: 25, FC: 48, Mol_Edit: 50) are similarly small, yet the paper draws strong qualitative conclusions from them.

Asymmetric rigor across methods: FT-Agent is run 3 times but all baselines (Manual SFT, OpenHands, Codex, Claude Code, backbone variants) are single runs, making the 'best on 10 of 13' comparison statistically unsupported. The Manual SFT baseline is additionally hobbled by an artificial 'Two-Pass' constraint, which inflates FT-Agent's relative standing.

Reported numbers are inconsistent across tables: e.g., FT-Agent Mol_Edit accuracy is 54.44 in Table 2 but 53.33 in Appendix Table 7; Vis Pass@1 is 29.33 in the text/Table 2 but 36.00 in Table 7; Finance QA differs between Table 2 (67.20) and Table 7 (67.53). Even if explained by single-run vs. 3-run means, this inconsistency is confusing and undermines confidence in the reporting pipeline.

The 'first interactive benchmark for end-to-end LLM fine-tuning' claim is overstated: MLE-Dojo (cited) is already interactive for MLE, and LaMDAgent (cited) uses agents for post-training pipeline optimization. The distinction (raw data repository, fine-tuning-only scope) is real but narrower than 'first' implies, and the benchmark itself is largely assembled from existing datasets (AIME, PANORAMA, ChemCoTBench, FinanceIQ, TableBench) plus LlamaFactory/OpenCompass wrappers.

FT-Agent's mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, feedback summarization, experience memory) are standard agentic patterns rather than a novel algorithmic contribution; the paper does not ablate the three claimed mechanisms individually, so the attribution of gains to the specific design choices is not established.

Narrow task regime relative to the framing: the benchmark restricts to SFT/LoRA with a 2,000-sample cap on a single 7B (or 3B) model, while the introduction frames the problem as production-grade end-to-end fine-tuning. RLHF/DPO, larger models, and multi-GPU settings are out of scope, limiting the significance of conclusions about 'autonomous LLM fine-tuning.'

Reproducibility concerns: the pipeline depends on frontier proprietary models (GPT-5.2 planning, GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini data synthesis, GPT-5 as AIME judge), which are neither stable nor widely reproducible; the implementation link promised in the abstract is missing, and the decontamination procedure is described only as 'rigorous' without specifics, despite DeepScaleR containing AIME problems from years adjacent to the 2025 test set.

Some experimental design details are questionable: data synthesis uses GPT-5 while GPT-5 is also the judge for AIME, a potential bias channel (albeit uniform across methods); the OpenHands baseline, while given identical tools, is wrapped in a scaffold whose design choices could themselves disadvantage it, and the 'cognitive gap' analysis (Appendix C.3) is interpretive rather than experimentally isolated.

Presentation issues: the manuscript text references 'Reviewers raised whether...' (§4.3), indicating rebuttal-era text left in the main paper; the task-definition formalism (Eq. 1) is essentially decorative; and several claims (e.g., 'enterprise-grade resilience features') read as marketing rather than technical content.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: end-to-end autonomous LLM fine-tuning (data construction + training configuration as joint optimization targets) is a genuine gap relative to MLE-Bench/MLE-Dojo/DSBench, and the paper clearly articulates how fine-tuning differs from traditional MLE tasks.

Solid benchmark engineering: sandboxed Docker execution, three well-defined interfaces (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator), two-phase validation/test protocol with strict leakage prevention and decontamination, and pluggable/extensible task design. The benchmark framing (Appendix A, 'Benchmark Framing') is honest that the contribution is the interactive protocol rather than the datasets themselves.

FT-Agent's three mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, structured feedback analysis) are concretely motivated by observed failure modes of general-purpose agents, and the fail-fast design is quantitatively supported (2.2x more effective iterations in Table 8).

Comparatively thorough evaluation for this area: controlled protocol holding tools/runtime fixed across agents, frontier-agent baselines (OpenHands, Codex, Claude Code), open-source planning backbones, 3-run statistics for FT-Agent, a 24-hour extended-budget check addressing a plausible confound, ablations over data scale/backbone/target scale, and validation+test results (Table 7, Table 11).

Honest limitations discussion: the Manual SFT baseline is explicitly scoped as constrained rather than a human upper bound, and the case studies candidly expose failure modes (shotgun debugging on PI4PC, data collapse on Visualization, causal reasoning deficits), which adds scientific value beyond headline numbers.
Reproducibility infrastructure appears substantial (prompt architecture in Appendix G, baseline harness details in Appendix B, code release promised).
weaknesses: Asymmetric statistical treatment: FT-Agent is run 3 times with mean±std, but all baselines (OpenHands, Manual SFT, frontier agents) are single runs. Several headline comparisons are within or near the reported FT-Agent variance (e.g., Reaction FTS 30.92±11.22 vs. OpenHands 35.59; Mol Und MAE 0.23±0.16), and the 'best on 10 of 13' claim is not statistically established.

Very small evaluation sets make many conclusions fragile: AIME has only 15 test instances (11.11% ≈ under 2 correct answers), Visualization 25, Fact Checking 48. Differences of one or two instances drive some qualitative claims (e.g., the 'breakthrough' on sparse supervision).

No component-level ablation of FT-Agent: the paper attributes gains to three mechanisms (planning, fail-fast validation, feedback analysis) but never ablates them individually against each other, so it is unclear which mechanism carries the improvement or whether a simpler combination suffices.

Potential judge/backbone coupling and bias: the agent backbone and data-synthesis models are GPT-5.2/GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini, and the AIME evaluator uses a GPT-5 judge; training data for chemistry is distilled from frontier models. This entangles FT-Dojo results with a specific commercial model family, and possible leakage from synthesis models to evaluation is not analyzed.

Internal inconsistencies across tables reduce confidence: FT-Agent AIME scores appear as 11.11±3.82 (Table 2), 13.33 (Table 4), and 20.00/13.33 (Table 10); OpenHands Vis Pass@1 is 24.00 in Table 2 but 8.00 in Table 11 validation; FT-Agent PI4PC validation differs between Table 7 (40.00) and Table 11 (38.67±2.31). These are likely explainable (single-run vs. mean) but the paper does not reconcile them.
Manual SFT comparison is heavily restricted (two-pass protocol, no LLM assistance), so the human-baseline comparison has limited informative value despite honest scoping.

Leftover revision artifacts weaken polish: 'Reviewers raised whether FT-Agent's gains...' in Section 4.3 is reviewer-facing text, and the implementation URL is blank in the abstract, undermining the reproducibility claim in the submitted version.
